summary:
Kursk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where the legal position for transgender visitors is prohibitive and has hardened since 2022. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression 'promoting' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the 'gay propaganda' law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Trans-specific healthcare and legal gender recognition were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents was signed.

The expanded propaganda statute reaches foreigners directly. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia, issued at Level 4, Do Not Travel, warns all travellers regardless of personal characteristic of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement, and states that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation. The advisory carries warnings specifically directed at LGBT travellers, and national government warnings to that effect are explicit.

A second layer of exposure applies nationwide, Kursk Oblast included. In 2023 the Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation, enabling criminal prosecutions carrying up to 12 years in prison on top of the 2013 propaganda law. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in that movement or displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, alongside 81 people convicted of administrative offences across 98 court cases since January 2024, most of them for symbols displayed on social media. Charges are brought under both the administrative and the criminal codes, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The volume of enforcement is rising with its severity. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, including convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside state action. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement regime is federal and uniform: the extremism designation, the propaganda statutes and the 2023 ban on gender transition operate in every subject of the Russian Federation, so no oblast-level variation in the governing rules can be relied on. Kursk Oblast offers no distinct legal shelter relative to other divisions.

The US advisory's wrongful-detention and arbitrary-law-enforcement warning is addressed to all travellers rather than to LGBT visitors alone, which means the same official risk of detention applies to a trans traveller's companions, colleagues and local contacts.

The trajectory of the regime is downward across the period covered by these sources: propaganda-law cases have grown eighteenfold over a decade, the 2023 extremism designation opened prison terms of up to 12 years, and raids moved from administrative fines into criminal territory within days of the court ruling.

Reporting on extreme coercive treatment of transgender people within Russia, including forced institutional confinement and enforced hormone administration, indicates risk from non-state actors as well as from police and courts.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kursk Oblast live under the same prohibitions as visitors, but with no option of departure as a mitigating measure: legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been unavailable since the 2023 legislation banning gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents.

Ordinary online conduct carries penalty. Most administrative convictions for displaying alleged LGBT movement symbols since January 2024 arose from social media posts, across 98 court cases and 81 convicted individuals.

Residents face the full criminal exposure of the extremism designation, with sentences up to 12 years' imprisonment for participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols, and repeat propaganda offences prosecuted criminally with up to four years' imprisonment.

Fines levied under the propaganda statutes function as a revenue line for the state budget, exceeding 60 million rubles ($765,300) over two years, which gives local enforcement authorities a direct financial incentive to continue issuing them.

State and family coercion intersect. The documented case of a transgender woman confined for nine months in a conversion-therapy facility and subjected to forced testosterone administration shows that relatives can initiate physical detention without state intervention, and that police response in that instance arrived only after the person obtained a phone.

LGBT+ people in Russia are recognised as a particular social group for the purposes of refugee-convention claims under UK asylum assessment, a standard that also covers residents of the Chechen republic.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kursk Oblast-specific enforcement data was located in this inventory. The counts cited (101 convictions, 81 administrative convictions, at least 139 people affected) are national totals, and the sources do not break them down by oblast, so the local frequency of propaganda or extremism charges in Kursk Oblast remains unresolved.

Whether Kursk Oblast has dedicated police units, designated prosecutors or local court practice targeting LGBT people is not sourced here; the assessment of uniform application rests on the nationwide scope of the federal statutes rather than on oblast-level reporting.

Entry and border-screening practice for transgender visitors arriving in or transiting through Kursk Oblast, including document checks and any risk of being identified from passport gender markers, is not addressed by these sources.

No sourced reporting on hate-crime violence against transgender people in Kursk Oblast, on the availability of legal, medical or shelter services for them in the oblast, or on local police responsiveness to complaints was located.

Conditions in the oblast arising from armed conflict and their effect on detention, movement and access to care are outside this inventory and are not verified here.
